_note: Which tradition counts which book as scripture. The 66 books follow their testament (see inc/canon.php); the books below are planned and have no text on the site yet. Lists vary between churches. Checked against the comparison tables in Wikipedia's 'Biblical canon' article (CC BY-SA 4.0) and the sources it cites.

jewish.name: Jewish
jewish.note: The Tanakh counts 24 books, the same writings as the Protestant Old Testament, arranged as Torah, Prophets and Writings.

protestant.name: Protestant
protestant.note: 66 books: the 39 of the Tanakh and the 27 of the New Testament.

catholic.name: Catholic
catholic.note: 73 books: the 66, plus the deuterocanonical books.

orthodox.name: Orthodox
orthodox.note: The Catholic books and more, based on the Septuagint; the lists differ somewhat between Orthodox churches.

ethiopian.name: Ethiopian
ethiopian.note: The widest canon. Authorities and printings differ on the list, and a narrower and a broader canon are distinguished.

sections.title: Deuterocanonical books
sections.intro: Books that the Catholic and Orthodox churches count as scripture and the Tanakh and most Protestant Bibles do not. Most survive in Greek, in the Septuagint.

books.name: Tobit
books.language: Greek; Aramaic and Hebrew fragments at Qumran

books.name: Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah
Additions to Daniel: Prayer of Azariah, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon
books.note: The Ethiopian Orthodox church is said to accept all the Catholic deuterocanonical books except the Maccabees.

sections.title: Further Orthodox books
sections.intro: Books found in Orthodox Bibles beyond the Catholic list. Which of them are canonical varies between Orthodox churches, and the Ethiopian Orthodox church shares several.

books.name: 1 Esdras
books.note: Ezra Kali in the Ethiopian canon.

books.name: Prayer of Manasseh
books.note: In the Ethiopian canon it is part of 2 Chronicles.

books.name: Psalm 151
books.note: The Ethiopian Orthodox church is said to accept the Orthodox additional books except the Maccabees.

books.name: 4 Maccabees
books.note: An appendix in some editions.

sections.title: Ethiopian Orthodox books
sections.intro: Books in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo canon beyond those above. The list varies between authorities, and a narrower and a broader canon are distinguished; books of the broader canon only are marked.

books.name: 1 Enoch (Henok)
books.note: Kept whole only in Ge'ez; Europe knew it only from Jude until James Bruce brought manuscripts in 1773.

books.name: Jubilees (Kufale)
books.note: Called Kufale in the Ethiopian church. The Ge'ez version is the only complete text.

books.name: 1 Meqabyan
books.note: Not the Maccabees of the Greek Bible.

books.name: Ezra Sutu'el (4 Ezra)
books.language: Latin and other languages; Hebrew original lost

books.name: 4 Baruch (Säqoqawä Eremyas)
books.note: In the Ethiopian canon it is part of Säqoqawä Eremyas.

books.name: Zëna Ayhud (Pseudo-Josephus)
books.note: Broader canon only. The church lists it as "The Book of Josephas the Son of Bengorion".

sections.title: Ethiopian Orthodox New Testament, broader canon
sections.intro: The broader Ethiopian Orthodox canon adds these church writings to the New Testament. They are not counted as scripture by any other church.

books.name: Sinodos (Ser'atä Seyon, Te'ezaz, Gessew, Abtelis)
books.note: Broader canon only. The church's own names: Sirate Tsion (order of Zion), Tizaz (the Herald), Gitsew, Abtilis. Contents vary between manuscripts.

books.name: Book of the Covenant (Mäshafä Kidan, two parts)
books.note: Broader canon only. The church lists it as two books, "The I book of Dominos" and "The II book of Dominos".

books.name: Ethiopic Clement (Qälëmentos)
books.note: Broader canon only. Not the Clement known in the West. The church lists it as "The book of Clement".

books.name: Ethiopic Didascalia (Didesqelya)
books.note: Broader canon only. Not the Didascalia known in the West. The church lists it as "Didascalia".

sections.title: Early Christian writings once read as scripture
sections.intro: No church counts these as scripture today. There was no fixed New Testament in the first century: for some centuries different churches read different writings as scripture, and these appear in early Bibles, canon lists or the writings of church fathers. Writings that were never put forward as scripture are left out.

books.name: 1 Clement
books.note: Written about the end of the first century. In Codex Alexandrinus, and listed as canonical in Canon 85 of the Apostolic Canons.

books.name: 2 Clement
books.note: A sermon of the second century. In Codex Alexandrinus, and listed with 1 Clement in Canon 85 of the Apostolic Canons.

books.name: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
books.note: A church manual of the first or second century; the dating is debated. Treated as scriptural by some early church writers; preserved in Codex Hierosolymitanus.

books.name: Epistle of Barnabas
books.note: Written between the late first and the early second century. In Codex Sinaiticus; also in the lists of Codex Claromontanus and Codex Hierosolymitanus.

books.name: Shepherd of Hermas
books.note: Written in the first half of the second century. In Codex Sinaiticus and in the list of Codex Claromontanus; read as scripture by some early church writers.

books.name: Apocalypse of Peter
books.note: Written in the early second century. Listed as accepted in the Muratorian fragment.

books.name: 3 Corinthians (from the Acts of Paul)
books.note: A second-century letter. Aphrahat and Ephraem treated it as canonical in the Syriac church; it was once part of the Armenian Bible.

books.name: Epistle to the Laodiceans
books.note: A short letter in Paul's name, in many Latin Vulgate manuscripts and in Wycliffe's English Bible.
